title: Love Lies Bleeding and wlw politics

commenti.body:
Reposting this from a previous- I loved how this film both sidestepped tropes and dug into ideas that aren't necessarily associated with this genre, or queer cinema in general. To me, it’s a film about toxic relationships, and how hard it is to escape them.

SPOILERS

>!At the start of the film, Lou is stuck in a small town. She and her father have done some very bad things in the past, and she no longer wants anything to do with him. She wants to leave, but her sister is in an abusive relationship that she’s not willing to leave, so out of concern for her, Lou stays, stuck in a dead-end town with little company except for her clingy, offputting ex, who she also tries to avoid, but presumably, when you’re a gay woman in a small US town in the 80s, you don’t have many options, so it’s harder to definitely end things with one of the only other queer women in town.!<

>!She’s also trying to quite smoking, but it’s hard to sever her relationship with cigarettes too.!<

>!Then Jackie rolls into town, and they hit things off. Everything’s going great between them at first, but the other problems in Lou’s life remain. Things start to spiral when Jackie snaps and murders Lou’s sister’s abusive husband (cue the Letterboxd “jawdropping” puns). This sets a chain of events in motion that include Lou leading the police to the evidence of her father’s crimes, and her father setting Jackie up to kill Lou’s ex.!<

>!Jackie shoots Lou’s ex (that plus the cops adding to Lou’s spiralling rug budget), and things come to a head when Lou is at her father’s mansion for a confrontation. At this point, I expected that we’d get the tragic BYGs conclusion with Jackie heroically coming to Lou’s rescue at the cost of her own life, but that’s not what happens. There’s a surreal, fantastical sequence of Jackie saving the day and the two running away together, and they both survive.!<

>!But then we cut to Lou in the car driving away, Jackie sleeping next to her. Lou then realises that her ex, rolled up in the trunk, is still alive. Jackie’s out for the count, so Lou has to pull over, finish the job by strangulation, and then drag her ex’s body to the side of the road to bury her.!<

>!Jackie was the woman who came into Lou’s life and got rid of her criminal father, her abusive stepbrother, her manipulative ex. But Jackie’s an impulsive, murderous, jealous, criminal with roid-rage. Lou has finally severed her old toxic relationships, only to replace them with another.!<

>!While Jackie sleeps soundly, oblivious to Lou’s struggles to finish dealing with the problems that Jackie herself caused, Lou stops, lights up a cigarette, inhales deeply, and sighs.​!<>!​!<

These are some great insights. I feel like cigarettes are something Lou tries to walk away from countless times but end up being something she seeks solace in for comfort after the tumultuous events. She can at least have that in the broken fairytale ending.

Thanks for sharing.

wlw = “women loving women”. 

“wlw politics” is being used as shorthand for queer film theory and analysis, specifically queer women’s film theory and analysis, specially queer sapphic women’s film theory and analysis. each one of those categories is its own field of study. 

saying “wlw politics” is the fastest, easiest way to indicate interest in this specific academic topic, similar to how “org-o” is typically used as shorthand for saying “organic chemistry”. it may appear to be inscrutable jargon to an outsider, but will be immediately understood by OP’s target audience. 

that doesn’t mean you’re being purposefully excluded from the conversation — those on the “inside” of a topic often fail to realize what is or isn’t “common knowledge” (insert relevant xqc comic here). you just have to do a quick bit of learning before jumping in.

hope that helps explain why op didn’t spell it out.

i’m sorry you’ve been interacting with people who make you feel that you “must” know certain things, or have made you feel excluded from certain discussions. if you can accept, without self-judgement, that you don’t know everything in the whole world, not knowing things stops feeling “exclusionary” and instead starts to feel like “an opportunity to learn something new”.
